6.2 — Ground Checks: No Infinite Jumps

Your jump works. That is the problem. Tap the key in mid-air and you jump again, and again, and again — a jump with no ground check is not a jump, it is a jetpack with infinite fuel. Today you teach the script to ask a question it has never asked: am I standing on something?

In this lesson you will be able to answer“why can I jump forever in mid-air?”Guided build
Break It Down~10 minGuided build

Your jump works — in mid-air, over and over, forever. "Why can I jump forever in mid-air?" is really "how does the script know it is standing on something?" Nothing on the Rigidbody2D means "grounded", no message fires when a foot touches a floor, and no message fires when it leaves one. So the whole feature is: decide what counts as ground, ask about it, and stop the jump until the answer is yes.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Make a bucket the physics engine can filter onA Ground layer in Edit ▸ Project Settings ▸ Tags and Layers, assigned to the tilemaps you can actually land on. A layer is not a tag: this cave's floor is already tagged Ground, and the second solid tilemap standing beside it is untagged — which is the whole argument for a bucket over a name.Read: the Layers list in Edit ▸ Project Settings ▸ Tags and Layers, and the tag-versus-layer callout in the first activity on this page
  2. Choose the point you will ask fromAn empty child object at the bottom edge of your collider, wired into a slot. Not the Player root: read Assets/Prefabs/Player and you will find the art on a child called Sprite at local position (0, 0.6, -1) and scale 2, so the root is not the middle of the character you can see. And the point has to sit outside your own collider, because this project ships Queries Start In Colliders ticked.Read: the [SerializeField] private Transform slot pattern from 1.3, and the Sprite child under Assets/Prefabs/Player — read its local position before you assume where the root is
  3. write this partRead: the Physics2D.Raycast page in the Unity scripting reference — an origin, a direction, a distance and a LayerMask, and a result that converts to true or false — plus the four-technique table in the middle of this page
  4. Stop the jump until the answer is yesThe jump line you wrote in 6.1 with one term added in front of it: it now needs the key and the ground. Two conditions in one if — the same folded && guard you wrote on the lever in 5.2, pointed at a fact about the world instead of a fact about an object.Read: the jump you wrote in 6.1, and the folded condition in the TryInteract() you built in 5.2
  5. Draw the question so you can see itA line from the check point, in the check direction, as long as the check distance — one colour when the answer is true and another when it is false. Three lines of gizmo code that turn "my jump does not work" into "my whisker is too short" in about four seconds.Read: the Gizmos.DrawLine and OnDrawGizmosSelected entries in the Unity scripting reference, and the Debug.Log habit from 3.3

Four of those five parts are work you have already done or already read: a [SerializeField] slot is 1.3, the jump line is 6.1, the folded && guard is 5.2, and a gizmo is a Debug.Log you can see without opening the Console. Only one part has no precedent at all, and it is the whole lesson. Every line this script has ever contained tells the engine to do something: move, add force, play a clip, destroy an object. A raycast is the first line that asks. And a question that nothing acts on changes nothing — which is exactly why the part after it is an if, and why those two parts are separate problems rather than one.

The test: could you look this part up on its own, right now, in one search? "Stop the infinite jump" cannot be looked up. "Send a ray straight down and find out what is on one layer" can — and the page you land on hands you four inputs in a fixed order and a result type that already knows how to say yes or no.

Your turn

Two of the four techniques in the table hand you a distance as well as a yes-or-no. Say what a game would do with that distance, and say whether your cave does it.

The answer your check produces is thrown away and computed again sixty times a second. Name the piece of state from 3.3 that worked the same way — and the piece of state in this lesson that deliberately does not.

The Problem: You Can Jump in Mid-Air ~15 min

Open Assets/_Scenes/Platformer.unity — the cave — and press Play. Jump once, then keep tapping the key while you are in the air. You climb. Nothing stops you, and the Console says nothing, because from the computer's point of view your code is working exactly as written: if the key went down, add an impulse. There is no rule about where you are allowed to do that.

Your goal: a jump that only fires when the character is standing on something. So start with the honest question — how would a script ever know it is standing on something? Nothing on the Rigidbody2D means "grounded". There is no event that fires when you touch a floor and another when you leave it. You have to go and ask.

The floor is already there. The question is not. Open the cave, expand Grid in the Hierarchy and select the Collision tilemap. It already carries a TilemapCollider2D, a CompositeCollider2D and a Rigidbody2D — and that body's Body Type is Static, which is why your character lands on it instead of falling through. Collision already works. What does not exist yet is any code that asks about it, and that is the entire lesson.

Read that body's Gravity Scale before you touch it. It says 1, and it is greyed out — and both of those are correct. Gravity Scale only means anything to a Dynamic body, because only a Dynamic body is moved by the physics engine. A Static body is never moved by anything, so Unity has nothing for that setting to do and disables the field. This is the same rule you met on the coin in 2.1 and again on the enemy in 4.1, seen from the other side: the body type decides who is allowed to move something, and the gravity scale only ever applies to the one type that is allowed. Do not "fix" the 1 — the moment you switch this tilemap to Dynamic, the ground starts falling.

Now count the surfaces. Under Grid there are three tilemaps — No Collision, Collision and Cave Exit — and only one of them carries the tag Ground. That single fact decides half of this lesson, so look at it properly before you read on.

There is a second solid object in this cave, and it is untagged. Select Cave Exit and read its Inspector: the same three components as the floor — a TilemapCollider2D, a CompositeCollider2D and a Static Rigidbody2D — and Untagged, because it was built to do a different job. SceneSwitch.cs sits on it, and when your collider touches it you are sent back to the Overworld.

So you have two solid surfaces and one tag between them. That is the difference between a tag and a layer, sitting in your own Hierarchy, and it is not a technicality: a tag answers "is this that one particular thing?" and a layer answers "is this the kind of thing I care about?". Only the second question still gives the right answer when somebody adds a third floor tilemap next week. You can compare a tag to a string; you can hand a layer to the physics engine and let it do the filtering.

Socratic: Asking Versus Remembering

  1. A tag and a layer are both just names attached to an object. Why can a raycast be told to ignore everything except one layer, but not "everything except one tag"?
  2. The Collision tilemap is tagged Ground and the Cave Exit tilemap beside it is not, and both of them are solid. If you wrote a ground check that compared tags, would it answer yes everywhere you can stand — and what would it cost you every frame you ran it?
  3. Your character is standing still on the floor. Is "grounded" a fact you could store when you land, or a fact you should re-check every frame? What could change it without any code of yours running?
Read the Docs: Four Ways to Ask About the Ground ~20 min

Every platformer ever shipped uses one of these. Read all four — the differences are in what each one can tell you and where each one lies to you. Then pick one, because you are going to live with the choice for the rest of the unit.

TechniqueThe question you are askingWhat it needsWhat it returnsWhere it lies to you
Physics2D.Raycast(origin, Vector2.down, distance, mask) "Is there a ground-layer collider directly below this exact point?" An origin (usually your feet, not your centre), a distance, and a LayerMask. A RaycastHit2D: the collider, the distance to it, the exact contact point and the surface normal. It is one infinitely thin line. Stand with one pixel of your feet over the edge of a tile and it reports air.
Physics2D.OverlapCircle(point, radius, mask) "Is there a ground-layer collider anywhere inside this circle at my feet?" A point, a radius, and a LayerMask. The collider only — no direction, no distance, no contact point. A wall beside your feet is inside the circle too, so you can be "grounded" against a vertical surface.
Collider2D.IsTouchingLayers(mask) "Is my own collider touching anything on this layer, right now?" Your Collider2D and a LayerMask. No origin, no distance, no ray. A single true or false. It can only see contacts that physically exist — a Kinematic body needs Use Full Kinematic Contacts ticked or it will report false while standing on the floor.
OnCollisionStay2D(Collision2D c) with a layer or tag check "What am I in contact with during this physics step?" A callback method, plus a rule to stop it re-firing your jump every step. The whole collision: the object, the contact points, the relative velocity. It fires continuously, so a naive jump fires continuously too; and it does not fire at all for a Kinematic body against static colliders unless full kinematic contacts are enabled. Even with them enabled you get the message, not a collision — the Kinematic body still passes through the static collider, which is why the full kinematic contacts checkbox is a way to hear a floor, never a way to stand on one.
Two names from the docs that are the same idea. A LayerMask field in the Inspector looks like a dropdown, but it is an integer whose bits mark which layers you care about. That is why "Everything" is not a special case in the code — it is simply all the bits switched on, which is exactly why it is the setting that produces the classic bug in a moment. And a tag is not a layer: the cave's floor already has the tag and the project has no matching layer at all, so the first thing you build today is not code.

Choose Your Check

  1. Which of the four did you pick, and which one does your character's body argue for? A character with a wide flat collider and one with a small round one do not fail the same way under the same technique.
  2. Two of the four can tell you how far the ground is. Which game behaviour needs that distance — and does your game have it?
  3. The circle check would call a wall "ground". Is that a bug you would fix, or a feature a wall-slide or wall-jump would later exploit?
  4. The collision-callback check needs no mask and no distance — it is the laziest to write. What does it demand instead, and which Rigidbody2D checkbox can silently break it?
Build It With MeGuided build

The question this answers“why can I jump forever in mid-air?”

You are editing Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs. Three Inspector fields, one empty child object, one method that asks a question every frame, and one term added to the jump condition you already have. The layer work is not code at all, and the raycast itself is a single line — that line is the one thing here with nothing earlier in the course to copy.

This build leaves 1 line for you to write. Everything around it is given, so you always know the shape of what you are producing.

Step 1Name the ground before you can ask about it — this step is not code

A mask is a filter, and a filter needs something to filter on. This project has the tag Ground and no Ground layer, so the first job is to make the bucket and put the right things in it.

// Edit ▸ Project Settings ▸ Tags and Layers  ▸  an empty User Layer  =  Ground

// Platformer ▸ Grid ▸ Collision      ▸ Layer = Ground
// Platformer ▸ Grid ▸ Cave Exit      ▸ Layer = Ground

// Platformer ▸ Grid ▸ No Collision  ▸ Layer stays Default
  1. 1Scroll the Layers list: Default, TransparentFX, Ignore Raycast, Water, UI, and a run of empty slots under them. Type Ground into the first empty one and close the window. Note what did not happen — no object in your project changed. A layer is a name for an empty bucket until something is put in it, and layers are project-wide, not per-scene, so you do this once for the whole game.A tag and a layer are not the same tool, and this project has been using the tag. The Collision tilemap is already tagged Ground, which is what a CompareTag check reads. A raycast mask cannot use a tag — it needs a layer — and there is no Ground layer in this project. Skip this step and the mask field you declare in step 3 has only Default and Everything to offer, and both of those include your own body.
  2. 3The cave floor and walls, and the thing your character has been landing on since 6.1. Read its Inspector while you are there: a TilemapCollider2D, a CompositeCollider2D, and a Rigidbody2D whose Body Type is Static. Collision already works — this lesson is not about making the floor solid, it is about asking the floor a question.Read that body's Gravity Scale before you judge it. It says 1, and it is greyed out, and both of those are correct. Gravity Scale is a multiplier on the gravity the physics engine applies to a body — and a Static body is never moved by anything, so there is nothing for the number to act on and Unity disables the field. It is the same rule you met on the coin in 2.1 and again on the enemy in 4.1, seen from the other side: the body type decides who is allowed to move something, and gravity only ever applies to the one type that is. Do not "fix" the 1 — switch this tilemap to Dynamic and the floor itself starts falling.
  3. 4The second solid object in this cave, and the one nobody remembers. It carries the same three components as the floor and the same Static body — and it is Untagged, because it was built for a different job: SceneSwitch.cs sits on it and sends you back to the Overworld when you touch it.This is the object a ground check written against a tag gets wrong, and it is why this lesson is about layers. Two solid surfaces, one tag between them. A tag answers "is this that one particular thing?", and a layer answers "is this the kind of thing I care about?". Put the floor in the bucket and leave the cave mouth out and your check is honest on everything you painted and guessing on everything else — silently, because a ray does exactly what its mask tells it to.
  4. 6Leave it alone. This tilemap is paint: a TilemapRenderer and no collider of any kind. A raycast reports colliders, and there is nothing here for one to report.

Step 2Put a point under your feet

A ray needs somewhere to start, and where you start it decides whether the answer is honest. Read your own prefab before you assume where the root is.

// Assets/Prefabs/Player ▸ the Sprite child ▸ read the Transform

// Assets/Prefabs/Player ▸ right-click ▸ Create Empty    rename it  GroundCheck
  1. 1Select the prefab asset in the Project window and look at its child called Sprite. Local position (0, 0.6, -1). Local scale 2. The art is not sitting on the root, and it is not centred on it either.So "fire the ray from the object's position" is a guess about a point you have never looked at. Every instinct says the root is the middle of the character; on this prefab the art hangs above the root, and your CircleCollider2D from 2.1 was dragged by hand until the green outline fitted that art. The collider — not the root, and not your memory of where you dragged it — is where the honest answer lives. Look at the green outline in the Scene view.
  2. 3Make it a child of the Player, then drag it in the Scene view until it sits on the bottom edge of your collider: centred in x, right on the line in y. It is a Transform and nothing else — no collider, no renderer, no script. It is not a thing in your game; it is a place to ask from.An empty child rather than an offset typed into the code. transform.position + Vector3.down * 0.6f is invisible, so "my whisker is in the wrong place" becomes an edit-and-recompile instead of a drag. There is a second reason and it is the one that bites: the ray must start outside your own collider. This project has Queries Start In Colliders ticked in Project Settings ▸ Physics 2D, so a ray that begins inside a collider reports that collider — for you, the Player, at distance zero, forever. That is the jetpack wearing a disguise.

Step 3Declare the point, the reach, the filter and the answer

Four lines in the class body, beside moveSpeed and the jump field from 6.1. Three are [SerializeField] knobs a designer can see in the Inspector — the pattern from 1.3 — and the fourth is the answer itself.

    [SerializeField] private Transform groundCheck;
    [SerializeField] private float groundCheckDistance = 0.1f;
    [SerializeField] private LayerMask groundLayer;

    private bool isGrounded;
  1. 1The slot that will hold the empty child from step 2. A Transform is a position in the world, and wired from the Inspector it is also a reference to another object — the same kind of slot as the waypoints in 4.1.Wire it at the end of this step, before you press Play. An empty slot does not complain when the scene loads; it throws a NullReferenceException at the first line that reads it, and this script reads it sixty times a second, so the Console fills faster than you can read it.
  2. 2How far down the ray reaches. 0.1 is a starting guess. The honest value is measured: the gap from the bottom of your collider to the tile surface, plus a hair.This number is the difference between a check and a lie, and you cannot read it off the screen. Too short and the ray misses the floor by a hair while your feet are visibly on it, so the jump stops working at random. Too long and the character is "grounded" while standing over thin air beside a ledge — the exact bug worth producing on purpose once.
  3. 3What the ray is allowed to notice. The type is LayerMask, not int, and the Inspector draws it as a dropdown of layer names rather than a number.A LayerMask is an integer whose bits mark which layers you care about — and that is the whole trick. It is why "Everything" is not a special case in the code: it is simply every bit switched on. Leave the field empty and the mask is Nothing, and a ray allowed to hit nothing reports nothing; point it at Everything and the ray is allowed to hit your own body.
  4. 5The answer, and the only thing in the file that changes because of it. Named for the question rather than the technique, so it reads correctly whether the answer came from a ray, a circle or a callback.In the class body — not inside the method that computes it. That is the scope rule from 1.3, and here it is load-bearing twice over: declared inside the method, it would be built and thrown away sixty times a second, and the jump in step 5 would read a name that does not exist when it looks. It is a field rather than a local for a second reason too: two different methods need it. The check writes it and the jump reads it, and a value two methods share is state.

Step 4Ask the question every frame

One call added to Update(), and one method that does nothing but ask. This is the part of the lesson with no precedent: every other line in this file tells the engine what to do.

        CheckGround();

    void CheckGround()
    {
        isGrounded = ____;
    }
  1. 1Called from Update(), beside your movement and your animation — the same shape as UpdateAnimation() and CheckAttack() from 1.6. It runs on every frame, and that is not an accident."Am I grounded" is a fact about right now, not an event that happened. Nothing in Unity sends you a message when a foot touches a floor and another when it leaves one. The closest thing you have met is the collision callback from 2.1 and 2.2, and those report contacts, not standing — a character leaning on a wall is in contact with it. So the honest value is the one you re-derive constantly. The third question of Asking Versus Remembering, above, is about exactly this.
  2. 3The method that asks. Empty parameter list, void, nothing handed back — everything it needs is a field from step 3. Same shape as UpdateAnimation() in 1.6: one idea, one method, so Update() stays readable as a list of things that happen each frame.
  3. Your turn5The whole lesson in one line, and the only line in this file that asks the engine a question instead of giving it an order. Fire the question down from the point you made in step 2, far enough to reach the floor, asking only about the layer you filled in step 1 — and store the yes-or-no answer in the field from step 3. All four inputs are in the four-technique table above, in the order they are written there. The method hands back a result object, and Unity's own documentation says that result converts to true when it hit something and false when it did not — which is why this line can end in a bool with no if anywhere in it.You want the Physics2D method that sends an infinitely thin line from a point, in a direction, for a fixed distance, and only reports what sits on the layers you hand it. The table above priced four techniques; this is the one with all four inputs and a result that carries the collider, the distance and the contact point. Pass them in the order the table writes them: the point from step 2, then straight down, then the distance field, then the mask field. A Vector3 position is accepted where the method asks for a Vector2, so groundCheck.position goes in as it is.Two things about this line are worth naming, because they are what make it a check rather than a trick. First, it is inside a method Update() calls every frame — not a one-off fired at the moment you land. Nothing would ever fire at the moment you stop landing, so a value stored once would be wrong from the first step off a ledge and would never correct itself. Second, it cannot change the game on its own. It writes a bool and touches nothing else: no force, no position, no animation. A question with no if in front of it is harmless, which is why the next step is where the jump stops working in mid-air.
  4. 6Closes CheckGround(). Nothing else in the file has changed yet — press Play now and the jump still fires in mid-air, because nothing reads the answer.

Step 5Make the jump wait for the answer

One term added to a line you already wrote in 6.1, and the infinite jump is over.

        if (isGrounded && Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space))
        {
            body.AddForce(Vector2.up * jumpForce, ForceMode2D.Impulse);
        }
    }
  1. 1The jump condition, now compound: two questions in one if. isGrounded is the new term; Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space) is the one-frame key check from 5.2, and it has to stay GetKeyDown — the Down is what makes one press one jump.Read the && in English before you trust it: "fire only if I am standing on something AND the key went down this frame". C# short-circuits, so on most frames isGrounded settles it and the key is never even looked at. And notice what that means for the player: a jump pressed in mid-air is not refused, it is thrown away — they have to press again after they land. That is a real complaint on a real playtest, and 6.3 is the lesson that stops throwing it away.
  2. 3The jump you wrote in 6.1, unchanged — your key, your force, your ForceMode2D.Impulse. Nothing about how a jump is performed changes today. Only when it is allowed to happen.This is the line the whole hour protects. One extra term in front of it, and a character that could climb the sky can now leave the ground exactly once per landing. That is the entire difference between a jump and a jetpack, and it cost one bool and an ampersand.
  3. 5Closes the jump method. One more } closes the class.

Step 6Draw the question, then prove the answer is honest

A check you cannot see is a check you will debug by guessing. Three lines of gizmo code turn that around, and four deliberate actions tell you whether to trust it.

    private void OnDrawGizmosSelected()
    {
        if (groundCheck == null) { return; }
        Gizmos.color = isGrounded ? Color.green : Color.red;
        Gizmos.DrawLine(groundCheck.position, groundCheck.position + Vector3.down * groundCheckDistance);
    }

// Player ▸ PlayerController  ▸  Ground Check = GroundCheck,  Ground Layer = Ground,  Ground Check Distance = 0.1
  1. 1A method Unity calls in the editor, not at runtime — nothing you write in here ships, and nothing in here can affect the game. It draws into the Scene view when this object is selected in the Hierarchy.
  2. 3The guard. During the frames before you wire the slot — and in any scene where you have not — groundCheck is nothing, and a gizmo that reads a position off nothing throws into the Console every frame you have the Player selected.
  3. 4One colour while the answer is true and another while it is false. The ? : is the conditional expression — the same yes/no branch as an if, written as a value, so it can be handed straight to Gizmos.color.Colour is the whole point, and it is not decoration. "My jump does not work" and "my ray is too short" look identical from the player's seat and completely different from the Scene view. A red line hanging in the air two centimetres above a green floor is a diagnosis.
  4. 5From the check point, straight down, exactly as far as the check reaches — the same three inputs the ray uses, drawn. If the drawn line and the real ray ever disagree, one of them is not reading the field you think it is.
  5. 6Closes the gizmo method.
  6. 8Wire the prefab, not one Player in a scene: drag the GroundCheck child into the slot, set the mask dropdown to Ground and nothing else, and type the distance you measured. Then press Play, keep the Player selected, and run the honesty test — stand still (green), jump (red the moment you leave the ground), land (green), walk off a ledge (red). If any of those four is wrong, your distance or your origin is wrong. Not your logic.
Check your work: the finished filetry every gap first — then open this to compare

Compare against your own file rather than copying it. The gap is the raycast assignment and it is the one line here with nothing earlier in the course to copy: a point, a direction, a distance and a mask, in that order. This version assigns the result straight into the bool, because a RaycastHit2D converts to true or false on its own — writing .collider != null on the end is equally correct and slightly more explicit, and either one passes. What has to match is the shape, not the text: the answer is computed in exactly one place, it is computed every frame rather than stored when you land, and the jump asks for it before it fires. Your field names, your key, your force and your movement method from 2.2 are all yours.

// ------------------------------------------------------------------
//  REFERENCE FILE — Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs
//  Written to be read, not pasted. Build it with the walkthrough
//  above, one step at a time, then open this and compare.
//  If it is sitting in your project unchanged, that is the thing
//  to go and do now — the walkthrough is still above you.
// ------------------------------------------------------------------
using UnityEngine;

// PlayerController.cs at the end of 6.2 — everything from 1.4 through 6.1,
// plus the one question this script has never asked: am I standing on
// something? Every other line here TELLS the engine what to do. CheckGround()
// ASKS it something, and CheckJump() is the only line that acts on the answer.
public class PlayerController : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private float moveSpeed = 5f;
    [SerializeField] private float jumpForce = 7f;          // yours, from 6.1

    // Today's three knobs, all visible in the Inspector (1.3).
    [SerializeField] private Transform groundCheck;              // where the ray starts
    [SerializeField] private float groundCheckDistance = 0.1f;   // how far down it reaches
    [SerializeField] private LayerMask groundLayer;              // what it may notice

    private Rigidbody2D body;
    private Animator animator;
    private SpriteRenderer spriteRenderer;

    // The answer. In the class body, because the check writes it and the jump
    // reads it — and re-derived every frame, because nothing ever tells you it
    // changed.
    private bool isGrounded;

    void Start()
    {
        // Looked up once, never inside Update() — the rule from 1.6 and 2.2.
        body = GetComponent<Rigidbody2D>();
        animator = GetComponentInChildren<Animator>();
        spriteRenderer = GetComponentInChildren<SpriteRenderer>();
    }

    void Update()
    {
        // ... your input, movement, gravity and animation lines from
        // 1.4, 1.6, 2.2 and 6.1, unchanged and left out here ...

        CheckGround();   // ask
        CheckJump();     // act on the answer
        UpdateAnimation();
    }

    // The whole lesson. A ray from the point under your feet, one direction,
    // one distance, one mask — and the result assigned straight into the bool,
    // because a RaycastHit2D converts to true when it hit and false when it
    // did not. Nothing here moves anything: a question is not an action.
    void CheckGround()
    {
        isGrounded = Physics2D.Raycast(groundCheck.position, Vector2.down, groundCheckDistance, groundLayer);
    }

    // The jump from 6.1 with one term in front of it. Leave the term out and
    // the character can climb the sky.
    void CheckJump()
    {
        if (isGrounded && Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space))
        {
            body.AddForce(Vector2.up * jumpForce, ForceMode2D.Impulse);
        }
    }

    // The same three inputs the ray uses, drawn. Keep the Player selected in
    // the Hierarchy while you play, and watch this go red the frame you leave
    // the ground.
    private void OnDrawGizmosSelected()
    {
        if (groundCheck == null)
        {
            return;
        }

        Gizmos.color = isGrounded ? Color.green : Color.red;
        Gizmos.DrawLine(groundCheck.position, groundCheck.position + Vector3.down * groundCheckDistance);
    }

    // ... UpdateAnimation(), CheckAttack(), the pickups and the damage, unchanged ...
}

// Edit ▸ Project Settings ▸ Tags and Layers:
//   the first empty User Layer  =  Ground
//
// Inspector, on Assets/Prefabs/Player ▸ PlayerController:
//   Ground Check            =  GroundCheck   <- an empty child sitting on the
//                                               BOTTOM EDGE of your collider
//   Ground Check Distance   =  0.1           <- measured, not guessed
//   Ground Layer            =  Ground        <- Ground, and nothing else
//
// The layer goes on BOTH solid tilemaps under the cave's Grid — Collision and
// Cave Exit. The third one, No Collision, has no collider at all, so no ray can
// ever hit it whatever layer it is on.
Build Lab: Prove It, Then Break It ~25 min

Step 1 — the honesty test. Press Play with the Player selected in the Hierarchy so the gizmo draws, and watch it through four deliberate actions: stand still (true), jump (false the moment you leave the ground), land (true), walk off a ledge (false). If any of those four is wrong, your distance or your origin is wrong — not your logic. Fix it by moving the empty child or changing the number, and run the four again.

Step 2 — walk the whole cave with the gizmo on. Find every place the line is red while your feet are visibly on something solid. Each one is a surface that is missing from your Ground layer — and there is at least one, because this cave has two solid tilemaps and only one of them was tagged. Decide which of the three tilemaps under Grid belong in the bucket and which one cannot possibly matter, and write the reason down before you tick anything.

Step 3 — the mask experiment. Set your mask to Everything and press Play. Stand still on the floor, then jump. If your origin sits inside your own collider, the ray hits you at distance zero and reports ground forever — the jetpack is back, and now it is wearing a disguise. Put the mask back to Ground and confirm the check is honest again. Then set it to Nothing and watch the opposite failure: a completely silent character who cannot jump at all.

Step 4 — tune the distance by measurement. Put the character on the floor, read the real gap from the bottom of your collider to the tile surface in the Scene view, and set the number from that. Then halve it, play, and watch the jump start failing on ground you can see. Guessing here is what produces exactly that failure.

Architectural specification: the check.
  • Which technique did you choose, and what are its exact inputs — origin, direction, distance, mask? If you chose anything other than the raycast the walkthrough built, describe how those four inputs map onto yours.
  • Where does the origin sit, and how did you find out rather than assume? The Player root is not the centre of the character you can see, and it is not automatically your feet.
  • How far is "down"? Measure the real gap from your collider's bottom edge to the tile surface, then write that number down. Guessing here is what produces a jump that fails at random.
  • Where does the mask come from — a serialized LayerMask field, or a hard-coded layer name? Which one lets a teammate fix your level without opening your script?
  • Where is the result stored, and what type is it? A bool named for the question ("am I grounded") reads better than one named for the technique.
  • Does the check run in Update() or FixedUpdate()? Remember that the answer is a physics answer, produced by physics, on the physics clock.
  • Is the jump condition now compound? Write the whole sentence in English before you write it in C#.
Architectural specification: making the invisible visible. Before you trust a check you cannot see, draw it. OnDrawGizmosSelected runs in the editor and can draw a line from your origin along your check direction, scaled by your distance. Three lines of code turn "my jump doesn't work" into "my whisker is too short" in about four seconds. Draw it in one colour when the check is false and another when it is true — and notice that drawing it costs your game nothing, because nothing in a gizmo method ships.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain the difference between a tag and a layer, using two solid tilemaps from your own cave as the example
  • Create a layer, assign it to every surface you can land on, and say which object must not get it — and why it cannot matter
  • Compare the four ground-check techniques and defend your choice
  • Show the check with a gizmo and tune the distance by measurement, not by guessing
  • Explain the self-hit bug, the Nothing mask, and why a LayerMask is what stands between you and both of them
  • Explain why the grounded value is re-derived every frame instead of stored when you land
  • Commit and push
